items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Deep Learning in Cadastral Mapping

items.content_html:
In this article, I explored how Artificial Intelligence and Deep Learning can contribute to the production, updating, and analysis of cadastral maps. I was particularly interested in the possibility of moving some of the traditionally time-consuming cadastral mapping tasks from manual digitization toward automated or semi-automated workflows.

Cadastral mapping is different from many other mapping applications because the geometry of land parcels has legal and financial implications. This makes accuracy, topology, and reliability particularly important. At the same time, converting old paper cadastral maps into digital data and extracting parcel boundaries from aerial imagery can require a significant amount of time and expert effort. These challenges motivated me to examine how recent developments in machine learning and computer vision could be applied to this field.

One of the main parts of the article is an overview of the relationship between Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning, with a focus on neural-network-based approaches for spatial data processing. I also discussed the concept of the Smart Cadastre, where spatial intelligence can be used to recognize and extract property boundaries and other land-related features from imagery.

[Insert Figure: Relationship between Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning]

I then reviewed several practical applications of AI in cadastral mapping. One example is the automatic conversion of scanned cadastral maps into digital vector data. In this type of workflow, image-processing and machine-learning techniques can be used to identify parcel boundaries, texts, parcel identifiers, and other cartographic elements. This approach can be particularly useful when large collections of historical maps need to be digitized.

[Insert Figure: Automatic extraction of cadastral information from scanned maps]

Another approach I examined was semi-automatic cadastral mapping from UAV imagery. In this workflow, the machine is responsible for identifying and classifying potential boundaries, while the operator remains involved in the final construction and validation of parcel polygons. I found this human–machine combination particularly interesting because it does not require complete automation; instead, it allows the strengths of both the algorithm and the expert to be used within the same workflow.

[Insert Figure: Cadastral map extracted from UAV imagery and comparison with the reference map]

I also reviewed the application of Deep Learning to 3D cadastral and building modelling. A case study from Tehran demonstrated how aerial imagery and Deep Learning could be combined to automatically extract buildings and subsequently generate their three-dimensional models. The workflow included aerial image preparation, image orientation, automatic building extraction, and 3D reconstruction. The results showed that Deep Learning can provide a practical way of processing large urban datasets where manual modelling would otherwise be extremely time-consuming.

[Insert Figure: Study areas in Tehran – Resalat and Sadeghieh]

[Insert Figure: Deep Learning architecture and example of input/output]

Another application discussed in the article is the detection of potential land grabbing by combining Deep Learning with cadastral and land-use data. In this approach, aerial imagery is first processed to produce land-cover and land-use information. These results can then be compared with cadastral information and public/private land records to identify areas where possible encroachment or unauthorized occupation may have occurred. This example shows that the value of AI in cadastral systems is not limited to map production; it can also extend to land administration, monitoring, and decision support.

[Insert Figure: Conceptual map of areas with potential land grabbing]

After reviewing these applications, I compared the performance of automated approaches with human operators. The results suggest that AI-based methods can provide a major advantage when large volumes of data need to be processed, particularly in rural and agricultural areas. However, in complex urban environments, manually produced boundaries can still provide better geometric and topological quality. This is an important distinction: the objective should not necessarily be to replace the cadastral expert, but rather to use AI where it can reduce repetitive work and improve the overall efficiency of the workflow.

[Insert Figure: Comparison of manually digitized and AI-derived cadastral data]

Based on the studies reviewed, I concluded that Deep Learning has considerable potential for the future development of automated cadastral systems. However, the quality of the final cadastral product still depends on the quality of the input data, the architecture and training of the model, and—most importantly—independent accuracy assessment. For large-scale applications, I also emphasized the importance of GPU-based processing because of the computational requirements of Deep Learning models.

Ultimately, I see Artificial Intelligence not as a replacement for surveying and cadastral expertise, but as a tool that can significantly change the way cadastral data is produced and maintained. Combining automated image interpretation with expert validation could provide a more scalable approach to cadastral mapping, especially as the volume of aerial and remote sensing data continues to grow.

items.title: Extracting Rural Cadastral Maps by Using Fully Automated Approaches Based on Artificial Intelligence

items.content_html:
Overview

This research is based on my Master’s thesis in Land Administration Systems at Shahid Beheshti University and Subsequently it is resulted a peer-reviewed research publication in the IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Applied Earth Observations and Remote Sensing (JSTARS).

It explores the application of Artificial Intelligence, deep learning, and high-resolution imagery for the automated segmentation of agricultural cadastral maps.

 

Abstract

Since one of the most fundamental challenges for land surveyors in Land Administration Systems is the production and updating of cadastral maps, the existence of a fully automated system that can digitize these maps using photogrammetry images would undoubtedly be very helpful. It can significantly reduce financial and human costs and expedite tasks.

Considering the emergence of deep learning models that leverage artificial intelligence for image processing and segmentation, I have undertaken to implement and execute a fully automated software equipped with a high-precision deep learning model for the production and digitization of cadastral agricultural maps.

To implement this approach, I first identified the necessary standards and common artificial intelligence models in this field. Then, by programming a fully automated approach and incorporating this model into it, I developed a program that can generate digital maps of agricultural lands solely by providing photogrammetry images. This approach consists of three main parts: image preprocessing, deep learning model processing, and image post-processing, all of which are implemented using Python programming in an open-source environment with open-source libraries and software.

One of the most important findings of this research can be the identification and utilization of the SAM model, which is one of the models for segmentation and identification of damages separately and has recently been introduced by Meta. During this research, this deep learning model was able to segment lands in some areas with an IoU accuracy of 92 percent.

In this research, it was determined that to improve the accuracy of results in such a fully automated approach, the use of Semantic Segmentation models like the U-net model is not suitable. On the other hand, to employ an Instance

Segmentation model like SAM, we need another accurate model to identify property parcels and provide a point from inside each agricultural land to the SAM so that this model can digitize only the desired parcels.

By: Nima Alimohammadi

Supervisor: Dr. Alireza Vafaeinejad

Workflow

The proposed workflow initialy was predicted in the sections of Data Preparation, Deep Learning Processing with Segmentation, and Post Processing with Image Segmentation.

However, after implementing and training a customized U-Net model specifically for my input data and processing the images with it, I realized that U-Net and other Semantic Segmentation methods were not suitable for this research, as neighboring fields could not be segmented separately by the model. Therefore, I implemented SAM (Segment Anything Model), developed by Meta (formerly Facebook), for the segmentation process.

I should add that I also tested some versions of SAM such as LangSAM and SamGeo, which their results didn’t cover all the agricultural fields on segmentation or hadn’t the result I was expecting, so I established the original SAM model like SamGeo for my application and re-implemented all codes for pre/post geospatial processing.

Methodology

01 - Data Preparation

I contaced European Space Agency for having access to their free satelite imagery for the research and they granted me their dataset access, but after considering the data I realized that the data’s resolution is not proper for rural cadastral maps and it could not result the minimum map scale accuracy, the 1:2000.

So I enrolled and requested Aerial Data from USGS.gov (United States Geological Survey) and chose some tiles of their accurate data from San Diego suburb.

As the chosen data contained infrared band and it was not a part of my research, because some fields were contain no vagetation and also I didn’t want to limit my model to the inferared band as the required input and let the user to use the system only with spectural bands (RGB), I eliminated it.

Then I rescale the images as thier resoulution were so high for a Deep Learning model. These all done while coordinate systems of the tiles should be save and transfered for new resoulution of the output spectural bands. I should add that all of these processes are through Python.

For the evaluation of the research I digitized the parcels of the tiles manually for the Ground Thruth layer to let me compare the AI Model result with a geospatial specialist result.

02 - Deep Learning Processing & Segmentation

I established the SAM model by using its pretrained weigths file. Then ran the system through a 12Gb graphic share by Google Colab and saved the output tiles with their input coordinate system as a segmented raster with randomized unique values for spectural bands of any parcel.

03 - Post Processing (Raster to Vector conversion)

The randomized value of colors of parcels helped me in this stage to vectorization the rasters and keep the neighbor parcels not merged.

04 - Evaluation

As the evaluation process needs prediction rasters (the output of the model) only in two deminssion of output pixels (0: not a field & 1: filed), I used the only red color band of the tiles and thresould them to binary output.

Then I prepared the ground truth with the same format rasters and coordinate systems of the prediction.

After all, I interseted and compared them with each other and resulted a dataset of 4 values of True Possitive, True Negative, False Possitive, and False Negative for pixels of any tile.

Predicted/Actual 1 (Possitive) -1 (Negative)
1 (Possitive) True Positive: 13,554,939 pixels False Negative: 7,520,258 pixels
-1 (Negative) False Positive: 891,848 pixels True Negative: 15,357,755 pixels

After all based on standard examination accuracy evaluation formulas of Deep Learning models, I assessed the system with IoU, Accuracy, Recall, Precision, and F1-score.

Results

The proposed approach demonstrated strong performance in areas where agricultural parcel boundaries were clearly identifiable.

These results demonstrate the potential of AI-based approaches for reducing manual intervention in large-scale cadastral map production.

They have been very helpful and inspiring to me, and they have taught me a lot of useful and interesting things in Deep Learning and Python. I am very grateful to have found such wonderful teachers and role models.
